item.research_question: How do crystal structure (FCC, BCC, FCC+BCC), temperature, and alloying elements influence the dry sliding wear rate, hardness, and coefficient of friction of high-entropy alloys?
item.material_system: Ingot cast high-entropy alloys including the Cantor alloy (CrMnFeCoNi) and its variations (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiTiAl, CoCrFeNiCu, CoCrFeNiS), categorized by FCC, BCC, and dual-phase (FCC+BCC) crystal structures.
item.processing_route: Manufacturing methods include arc melting (most common), vacuum arc melting, induction melting, and spark plasma sintering (SPS); ingots are remelted multiple times for homogeneity, and composites are prepared by mixing powders (e.g., with MoS2, graphite, Ag) before sintering.
item.test_conditions: Dry sliding conditions using ball-on-disk, pin-on-disk, and ball-on-block setups; counter bodies include Si3N4, Al2O3, and steels (SKH51, 100Cr6, GCR15); tests conducted at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 600°C and beyond); loads and sliding velocities varied (e.g., 5 N, 0.28 m/s).
key_findings: HEAs with a BCC structure showed superior hardness and wear properties compared to FCC and FCC+BCC alloys due to reduced ductility and limited slip systems.
The addition of Al and Ti to the Cantor alloy increased hardness by up to 40% and promoted a transition from FCC to harder BCC phases.
Wear rates for most HEAs decreased after reaching a certain elevated temperature due to the formation of a protective oxide layer at the sliding interface.
The addition of 0.2 to 1 at.% Cu to CoCrFeNi HEA reduced the wear rate at 600°C by 40–45% due to the lubricating nature of Cu at high temperatures.
Self-lubricating composites with MoS2 and graphite showed significantly lower coefficients of friction but higher wear rates above 200°C compared to the base SPSed HEA.
FCC phase HEAs exhibited higher coefficients of friction and lower hardness compared to BCC phase HEAs, resulting in larger wear tracks.
The addition of V increased hardness but subsequently increased the wear rate after a certain percentage was added.
item.mechanism: The superior wear resistance of BCC phases is attributed to limited slip systems causing strong but brittle behavior. At elevated temperatures, wear reduction is driven by the formation of a protective oxide layer (tribo-oxidation) or self-lubricating phases (e.g., CrxSy, sheared Cu) that reduce friction and protect the surface. The 'cocktail effect' and lattice distortion contribute to solid solution strengthening and high hardness.
item.limitations: The review notes that intrinsic brittleness in BCC alloys is a trade-off for wear resistance. The oxidation mechanisms are complex due to multiple elements, and the influence of individual elements can taper off or become ill-advised at certain ratios (e.g., excessive brittleness from C or Cr3C2). Manufacturing homogeneity is challenging due to varying densities and melting points.
item.future_work: Future studies should focus on understanding tribo-oxidation behavior in different environmental conditions, creating guidelines for selecting solid lubricants, exploring additive manufacturing techniques (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) for HEA composites, and conducting detailed cost-performance matrix studies against conventional alloys.
quotes: In general, HEAs with a BCC structure showed superior hardness and wear properties compared to FCC and FCC + BCC alloys.
The lesser wear rate of HEAs with a BCC structure is attributed to the reductions in ductility, resulting in strong but brittle alloys.
